title: Develop, execute, and manage notebooks - Microsoft Fabric
summary: Microsoft Learn's reference for authoring and running Fabric notebooks, covering the multi-language cell model that underpins Spark SQL usage: the %%sql and other language magic commands, IntelliSense support per language, %run for referencing notebooks and .sql script files, and the %%configure session magic (including a Spark-SQL-specific row-limit setting). A supporting fact on how the pinned default lakehouse determines which Hive metastore Spark SQL resolves table names against is drawn from Microsoft's companion lakehouse-notebook-explore page.
audience: Data engineers and analysts writing Spark SQL in Fabric notebooks, and platform admins configuring per-session Spark/SQL behavior.
why_it_matters: Fabric notebooks are polyglot by cell, not by notebook, so knowing exactly which magic switches a cell into Spark SQL — and what that gives you versus PySpark or Scala cells in the same session — is a prerequisite for writing correct, maintainable lakehouse notebooks. It also explains the less obvious mechanics: how the default (pinned) lakehouse silently decides which metastore unqualified table names resolve against, and how session-level SQL behavior (like result row caps) is tuned outside the SQL itself.
takeaways: Spark SQL is one of four first-class per-cell languages in a Fabric notebook, switched in via the %%sql magic (or the cell language picker), alongside %%pyspark, %%spark (Scala), and %%sparkr.
SparkSQL cells get IntelliSense syntax highlighting, error marking, and completion, but not user-defined-function completion — a smaller feature set than PySpark/Scala/SparkR cells get.

The pinned default lakehouse in a notebook determines which Hive metastore Spark SQL resolves unqualified table names against, so mixing lakehouses from different workspaces in one notebook is an easy source of 'table not found' errors.
The %%run magic can execute a stored .sql script from a notebook's built-in resources, not just Python, letting teams keep reusable Spark SQL logic in versioned .sql files.
Spark SQL session behavior (such as the number of rows returned) is tunable outside the query text via the %%configure magic's conf block, e.g. the livy.rsc.sql.num-rows setting.
%%sql is one of only five magic commands Fabric pipelines support when running a notebook activity, so pipeline-triggered notebooks have a narrower magic surface than interactive ones.

claims.text: Fabric notebooks support four Apache Spark cell languages — PySpark (Python), Spark (Scala), Spark SQL, and SparkR — switched per cell with a language magic command (%%pyspark, %%spark, %%sql, %%sparkr) placed at the top of the cell, or via the cell language picker, independent of the notebook's overall primary language.

A %%sql cell executes its query as SparkSQL against the notebook's Apache Spark context, not against a separate SQL engine, so it shares the same running Spark session, cluster, and attached lakehouse as PySpark or Scala cells in that notebook.

IntelliSense support in Fabric notebooks differs by cell language: SparkSQL gets syntax highlighting, error marking, syntax and variable/system-function code completion, smart indent, and code folding, but explicitly lacks user-defined-function code completion, a gap that PySpark, Scala, and SparkR cells don't have.

The pinned default lakehouse of a notebook determines which Hive metastore Spark SQL queries resolve unqualified table names against; when a notebook has multiple lakehouses attached, the lakehouse being queried with Spark SQL must be in the same workspace as the current default lakehouse or resolution fails.

The %run magic command can execute a stored Python or SQL script file from a notebook's built-in resources (for example %run -b script_file.sql), so reusable Spark SQL logic can be version-controlled as a .sql resource file and invoked from any notebook in the same session rather than being copy-pasted into cells.

The %%configure session-configuration magic accepts a Spark-SQL-specific conf setting, livy.rsc.sql.num-rows, that controls how many rows a Spark SQL query returns to the notebook, illustrating that SQL-cell behavior in Fabric notebooks is tuned through session configuration rather than SQL syntax like LIMIT alone.

When a notebook runs as a Fabric pipeline activity rather than interactively, only five magic commands are supported: %%pyspark, %%spark, %%csharp, %%sql, and %%configure — a materially narrower set than the full magic-command list available in interactive notebook sessions.

Custom notebook-defined magic commands can be authored in one notebook (for example a 'MyLakehouseModule' notebook) and referenced from another notebook, letting teams package Spark SQL or PySpark helper logic behind a shared magic invoked across notebooks of possibly different primary languages.
